report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **well-supported by evidence**. The largest and most rigorous trial, a randomized controlled study of over 1,000 women (Tuuli et al., NEJM, 2016), found chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation significantly reduced surgical-site infection (SSI) after cesarean delivery compared with iodine-alcohol (relative risk ~0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90), roughly halving infection risk, including both superficial and deep incisional infections (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

This finding is corroborated by subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses pooling multiple RCTs. A 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis specifically comparing chlorhexidine-alcohol with povidone-iodine for cesarean delivery found a significant reduction in SSI risk with chlorhexidine-alcohol (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52–0.98), with no heterogeneity across studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/). A more recent network meta-analysis of RCTs in cesarean sections similarly concluded that alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being the most effective antiseptic for preventing SSI, ahead of alcohol-based povidone-iodine (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282).

Some smaller individual pilot trials have shown a trend favoring chlorhexidine-alcohol without reaching statistical significance, but these are consistent in direction with the larger trials and meta-analyses (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/).

**Overall**: The preponderance of high-quality evidence, including the pivotal NEJM RCT and multiple meta-analyses, supports the claim that chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation reduces SSI after cesarean delivery compared with iodine-alcohol. This has led major guidelines to recommend chlorhexidine-alcohol as the preferred preoperative antiseptic for cesarean sections.
